title: Type safety
cards/0/body:
A type says what's stored in memory: a number, a string, an array. Type-safe code touches memory only in ways the type allows: it doesn't read a string as a number or step past the end of an array.

That protects objects from each other, against both honest mistakes and attacks.
cards/1/body:
According to the Microsoft article, the CLR relies on three rules for type-safe code:

1. A reference to a type is always compatible with that type.
2. Only the operations defined for an object are invoked on it.
3. An object is what it claims to be.
cards/2/pairs/0/0: Reference is compatible with its type
cards/2/pairs/0/1: A string is read as an array of numbers
cards/2/pairs/1/1: A number gets a method call it doesn't have
cards/2/pairs/2/0: An object is what it claims to be
cards/2/pairs/2/1: An object poses as a different type
cards/3/options/0: InvalidCastException: the CLR won't let a string pass as an array
cards/3/options/1: a ends up holding the character codes
cards/3/explain: The compiler lets it through: an object could be anything. But at run time the CLR checks the real type and throws.
cards/3/wrong/2: It compiles: casting object to int[] is legal until it turns out there's a string inside.
cards/4/options/1: It writes 1 into the memory past the array
cards/4/explain: The CLR checks array bounds on every access. Safe code can't write past the end.
cards/4/wrong/1: That could happen in C or C++. In managed code the CLR won't let you cross the bound.
cards/5/body:
Before JIT compilation, CIL went through verification: can we prove the code is type-safe? If security policy required verified code and the check failed, you got an exception at startup.

The verifier plays it safe: it also rejects some code that is safe. For example, any code with pointers (unsafe).
cards/6/q: Which line would the verifier reject?
cards/6/explain: A pointer means unsafe code. Here it's actually harmless (the address of a local variable), but the verifier can't prove that, so it rejects any code with pointers.
cards/7/q: What does verification check? Select all that apply.
cards/7/options/0: Memory is accessed through the correct types
cards/7/options/1: The CIL is well-formed, e.g. the stack has enough numbers
cards/7/explain: Verification is about memory safety and well-formed CIL. It doesn't check program logic.
cards/8/body:
.NET Core and .NET 5+ dropped the old security policy system (CAS), and the CLR does not verify CIL at startup.

Type safety now rests on the compiler and run-time checks: array bounds and type casts, exactly what you just saw. You can check CIL by hand with the ILVerify tool.
cards/8/deep: That's why unsafe code in modern .NET simply runs if the project allows it (<AllowUnsafeBlocks>). The responsibility is on the programmer. Untrusted code is now isolated with processes and containers, not inside the CLR.
cards/9/q: Remember the broken CIL from lesson 3 (add with only one number on the stack)? What would the .NET Framework verifier do with it?
cards/9/options/0: Reject it: that CIL is invalid
cards/9/explain: Checking that CIL is well-formed is exactly the verifier's job: badly generated CIL breaks the safety guarantees.
